messages.content:
Write ONE original fictional document, not JSON and not multiple versions.
Return only the complete document. It MUST contain 1400 to 1600 words of substantive content.
Use twelve connected paragraphs of roughly 100 words each and a numbered section with four
substantial items. Do not stop after an outline or summary. This length is required because
the small rewriter must learn to preserve information across a full long document.
Use the supplied fictional situation. Expand it with internally consistent concrete details,
uncertainty, conditions, and follow-up requests. Include all protected anchors exactly, with
the quoted line inside a direct quote. Keep quotes and code/path literals exact.
For /slack write a long casual team message. For /transcribe write a long, clean spoken account,
with natural conversational wording. For /prompt write a detailed REQUEST for a useful task,
including background and all constraints; do not perform the task. For /polish write clear plain
prose. Do not mention a formatter, dataset, word count, mode, or these authoring instructions.
Preserve the feature guidance. Include a numbered section, full paragraphs, a direct quote,
and a condition that refers to information elsewhere. Make the final paragraph substantive.

{"id": "sft-v1-coin-club-transcribe-long-v3", "source_group": "sft-v1:coin-club", "split": "validation", "mode": "/transcribe", "brief": "a coin collector club's display arrangements", "situation": "Dario is checking 151 display holders for a coin collector club's display arrangements. An attached note reads 'Keep the two holders apart.' and must be quoted as data. The count has not been confirmed. An additional action is allowed only after the count is checked. The writer wants a specific follow-up rather than a generic description.", "language": "en", "length": "long", "feature": "condition", "anchors": ["Dario", "151 display holders", "Keep the two holders apart.", "coin-club_2.txt"], "context": {}, "authoring": "canonical_extended", "word_range_per_string": "1400 to 1600", "mode_contract": "Remove true hesitation and accidental restarts. Apply explicit corrections to the final stated intent. Preserve meaningful filler-like words and unfinished thoughts. Apply clearly spoken punctuation and list cues. Keep the supplied language.", "feature_guidance": "Include a condition that limits a request; preserve it in every variant."}

result.text:
Dario is checking the display arrangements for the coin collector club, and I want to explain what we know so far without making the count sound more certain than it is. There are 151 display holders in the working list, but that number has not been confirmed against the actual holders. He is going through them one at a time, checking which pieces are present and whether each holder is assigned to the right part of the display. Until that check is finished, we should treat 151 as the number under review, not as a verified inventory total. That distinction matters for the arrangement and for any follow-up decision.

The attached note is relevant to one particular placement question. It reads, “Keep the two holders apart.” I am quoting that wording as it appears, rather than treating it as a general instruction to spread all the holders across the room. We still need to establish which two holders the note refers to and whether the note applies to the current display plan. The wording is clear about keeping a pair apart, but it does not name the pair, say how far apart they should be, or specify whether the separation is for handling, security, presentation, or another reason. Those details remain open.

The file connected to the note is coin-club_2.txt. We should check that file for any context that identifies the two holders or explains why they must remain separate. If the file contains a clear identification, Dario can compare it with the physical labels while he is checking the inventory. If it does not, we should not guess which pair was intended. In that case, the specific follow-up should be a question to the person who supplied the note, asking them to identify the two holders and clarify whether the instruction still applies to this arrangement. That would resolve the uncertainty without changing the note’s meaning.

For the moment, Dario’s immediate task is limited to checking the count and recording what he finds. He should note any holder that is missing, damaged, unlabelled, or in a different location from the current arrangement sheet. He should also record whether each holder is already positioned on a display surface or is still being stored separately. Those observations may help explain a difference between the list and the physical count. They should not be used to silently revise the list, though; the club needs a clear record of what was originally listed and what Dario actually verified. If he finds a mismatch, the mismatch should be reported before anyone updates the total.

I want the follow-up to be concrete rather than just asking for a general description of the display. First, please ask Dario to send the verified count once he has finished checking all the holders. Second, ask him to say whether he found any missing, damaged, unlabelled, or misplaced holders, and to identify those by their existing labels where possible. Third, ask him to confirm whether the two holders mentioned in the note can be identified from coin-club_2.txt or from labels on the holders themselves. If he can identify them, he should report their labels and their current locations. If he cannot, we need to ask the note’s author for clarification instead of choosing a pair ourselves.

There is an important condition on any additional action: it should happen only after the count has been checked. Until then, we should not move holders to new positions, print a revised arrangement, or tell club members that the total is confirmed. The one exception is ordinary care needed to keep the items safe while Dario checks them; that does not authorize a new display plan. Once the count is checked, we can consider an additional step, but only if the verified count and the identification of the two holders give us enough information to do it responsibly. If either point is still unresolved, the next action should be a clarification request, not a rearrangement.

For the count check, it would help to use a simple, consistent method. Dario can start at one end of the storage or display area, inspect one holder at a time, and mark each item on the current list only after seeing it. If a holder has no legible label, he can record its location and a short neutral description without assigning it a new identity. At the end, he should compare the marked list with the number physically checked. A second pass would be useful if the checked total differs from 151, or if he has to leave and resume later. We should not require an unnecessary second count when the list and the physical total match and the record is clear.

The club should also avoid treating a placement question as a count discrepancy. Two holders might be intentionally kept apart while still both being included in the total. Conversely, a holder might appear in the list but be stored elsewhere, so it is not available for the planned arrangement even if it exists. Dario’s report should distinguish those cases. It can say how many holders he physically checked, whether that equals the working figure of 151, and whether any listed holders were not available in the display area. That will give the club a more useful picture than a single number without context, especially if the next step depends on which pieces are ready to be displayed.

The note itself should remain attached to the record while the question is being resolved. We should preserve its exact text, including the phrase “Keep the two holders apart.”, and avoid rewriting it as though it named specific pieces. If someone later confirms which holders it means, that clarification can be added as a separate note with the source and date, rather than replacing the original wording. This is especially useful if the arrangement changes in the future or if a different volunteer takes over. Keeping the original instruction and the later explanation distinct makes it easier to understand what was known at each stage and reduces the chance that a guess will be mistaken for a confirmed decision.

Here is the follow-up I would send to Dario, in a direct and practical form: “Please finish checking the 151 display holders against the current list and let us know the verified count. If the total is different, or if any holders are missing, damaged, unlabelled, or stored somewhere unexpected, please identify those items and describe where you found them. Please also check coin-club_2.txt and the holder labels to see whether they identify the pair covered by the note, ‘Keep the two holders apart.’ If they do not identify the pair, please say so, and we will ask the note’s author for clarification. Please do not make a new arrangement until the count has been checked.” That request gives him a defined task and a clear stopping point.

For clarity, the response does not need to solve every display issue at once. The first decision is whether the working count is accurate. The second is whether the note can be tied to two identifiable holders. After those answers are available, the club can decide whether it has enough information to make an additional change. If the count is confirmed but the pair is still unknown, we can keep the current positions and ask the author to clarify. If the pair is known but the count remains uncertain, we should still wait before preparing a revised plan. If both are confirmed, Dario can recommend a placement that respects the note, but the club should approve that change before it is treated as final.

It would also be useful for Dario to report when and where he completed the check, because that helps explain the result if the display is later moved. He does not need to provide a long account of every holder if everything matches. A short confirmation with the checked total, the location checked, and any exceptions will be enough. If there are exceptions, the labels and locations matter more than a general statement that something looked wrong. Where a label is unreadable, he can say that plainly and describe the holder without guessing at its contents. The goal is a record another club member can follow, not a new catalogue or an unsupported interpretation of the note.

So, for now, the arrangement remains provisional. Dario is checking the listed 151 display holders, but the count has not yet been confirmed. The attached instruction says, “Keep the two holders apart.”, and coin-club_2.txt should be checked to see whether it identifies the pair. Please ask Dario for the verified total, any specific exceptions, and the labels and locations of the two holders if he can determine them. If the file and labels do not make the pair clear, ask the note’s author directly. Only after the count is checked should the club consider an additional action; if the count or the pair remains unclear, keep the current arrangement and request the missing information first.
